items.readable_text:
Content:
How do we calculate [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\to\infty}\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)] and [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\to-\infty}\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)?] To find out, let's look at the graph of [MATH: y=\dfrac{1}{x}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b6a797f2a07b1cb03ccd7b86bac613ca]

Content:
We see that the curve approaches zero as [MATH: x] approaches positive infinity. The same is true as [MATH: x] approaches negative infinity. So, we write
[MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to \infty} \left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)=0 \qquad \textrm{and} \qquad \lim_\limits{x \to -\infty} \left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)=0.]

Content:
The same is true for [MATH: \dfrac{1}{x^n}] where [MATH: n] is any positive integer. For example,

Content:
[MATH: lim_(x → ∞)((1)/(x^{2})) = 0|andlim_(x → − ∞)((1)/(x^{2})) = 0; lim_(x → ∞)((1)/(x^{3})) = 0|andlim_(x → − ∞)((1)/(x^{3})) = 0; ⋮]

Content:
and so on. This is because as the size of [MATH: x] increases, the size of [MATH: \dfrac{1}{x^n}] decreases.

items.title: Limits at Infinity of Reciprocal Functions

sections.readable_text: Compute [MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{4x^4}.]
EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we use the algebra of limits to pull out the constant factor of [MATH: \dfrac 1 4\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: lim_(x → ∞)(1)/(4x^{4})|= lim_(x → ∞)(1)/(4) ⋅ (1)/(x^{4}); = (1)/(4) ⋅ lim_(x → ∞)(1)/(x^{4})]

Now, using the fact that

[MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to \infty} \left(\dfrac{1}{x^4}\right)=0,]

we can evaluate our limit as follows:

[MATH: \dfrac{1}{4} \cdot\lim_\limits{x \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{x^4} = \dfrac 1 4\cdot 0 = 0]

For example, the expression [MATH: x^3 - x^2 + 1] is a non-constant polynomial, so we have

Content:
[MATH: \lim_{x\to\pm\infty}\left(\dfrac{1}{x^3 - x^2 + 1}\right) = 0.]

Content:
Likewise, the expression [MATH: (2x-5)^4] can be multiplied out to become a non-constant polynomial, so we have

Content:
[MATH: \lim_{x\to\pm\infty}\left(\dfrac{1}{ (2x-5)^4 }\right) = 0.]

Item 9 — Tutorial: Infinite Limits of Reciprocal Functions Where the Leading Term Has an Odd Power

Content:
Let's again look at the graph of [MATH: y=\dfrac{1}{x}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b6993678c5aa3e224e42b0167620a04a]

Content:
From the graph, we see that

Content:
[MATH: \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 0^-} \left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right) = -\infty \qquad \textrm{and} \qquad \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 0^+} \left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right) = \infty.]

Content:
Since the left and right-sided limits are not the same, we conclude that

Content:
[MATH: \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 0} \left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right) = \textrm{DNE}.]

Content:
Any function of the form [MATH: y = \dfrac{1}{x^n},] where [MATH: n] is an odd natural number, has the same shape as [MATH: y = \dfrac{1}{x},] and consequently the limit behavior is the same. For example,

Content:
[MATH: lim_(x → 0^{−})((1)/(x^{3})) = − ∞,|lim_(x → 0^{+})((1)/(x^{3})) = ∞,; lim_(x → 0^{−})((1)/(x^{5})) = − ∞,|lim_(x → 0^{+})((1)/(x^{5})) = ∞,; ⋮]

Content:
and so on. For all of the above, the limit of the function does not exist at [MATH: x=0] because the left and right limits are not the same.
